center.name: Vice Admiral Takeo Kurita
center.role: Commander, First Diversion Attack Force (Center Force)
center.bio: A cautious, experienced surface officer who had commanded cruiser divisions since Java Sea. Swam for his life when Atago went down under him on 23 October, then led the surviving fleet through San Bernardino Strait. His decision to break off the pursuit off Samar at 09:20 — believing he faced Halsey's fleet carriers — remains one of the most debated calls of the war.

southern.name: Vice Admiral Shōji Nishimura
southern.bio: Ordered to force Surigao Strait and reach Leyte Gulf at dawn in concert with Kurita, he pressed on through PT-boat and destroyer attacks into the guns of six battleships, despite knowing Kurita had been delayed. Made no attempt to coordinate with Shima's force following behind.
southern.fate: Went down with Yamashiro at 04:19 on 25 October.

shima.name: Vice Admiral Kiyohide Shima
shima.bio: Arrived in Surigao Strait 40 minutes behind Nishimura to find burning wreckage. After Nachi collided with the crippled Mogami he judged the battle lost and withdrew — the only Japanese admiral at Leyte to retreat with his force largely intact.

northern.name: Vice Admiral Jisaburō Ozawa
northern.bio: Commanded the carrier force at the Philippine Sea and now led the near-empty carriers north as bait. His plan worked perfectly — Halsey took the whole of TF 38 after him — at the cost of all four carriers. Regarded by both sides as one of the ablest Japanese admirals of the war.
northern.fate: Survived; last commander of the Combined Fleet. Died 1966.

taffy3.name: Rear Admiral Clifton A. F. Sprague
taffy3.bio: "Ziggy" Sprague found four battleships and eight cruisers on his horizon at dawn and fought them for two and a half hours with six escort carriers, three destroyers and four destroyer escorts. His handling — running into the wind to launch, then turning into rain squalls and smoke while his escorts charged — is a textbook of small-ship tactics.
taffy3.fate: Died 1955; USS Clifton Sprague named for him.

tg383.name: Rear Admiral Frederick C. Sherman
tg383.bio: Fought off three land-based raids on 24 October (losing Princeton) while striking Kurita, then located Ozawa that afternoon. His group led the strikes off Cape Engaño.

tg382.name: Admiral William F. Halsey Jr.
tg382.role: Commander, Third Fleet (embarked in New Jersey with TG 38.2)
tg382.bio: Aggressive to a fault, Halsey took every carrier and fast battleship north after Ozawa on the night of 24 October, leaving San Bernardino Strait unguarded. Nimitz's query — "Where is, repeat, where is Task Force 34? The world wonders" — reduced him to tears of rage. He turned south too late to catch Kurita.

tg384.name: Rear Admiral Ralph E. Davison
tg384.bio: His Enterprise aircraft found and attacked Nishimura in the Sulu Sea on the morning of 24 October, then his group joined the run north.

tg381.name: Vice Admiral John S. McCain Sr.
tg381.bio: Recalled while steaming to Ulithi, he launched strikes at Kurita from 335 nautical miles on 25 October — the longest carrier strike of the war — and harried the retreating Center Force on the 26th.
tg381.fate: Died 1945, four days after the Japanese surrender.

tg772.name: Rear Admiral Jesse B. Oldendorf
tg772.role: Commander, Task Group 77.2 (Bombardment and Fire Support Group)
tg772.bio: Laid a textbook trap across Surigao Strait: PT boats, then destroyers, then six battleships — five of them Pearl Harbor survivors — crossing the T of Nishimura's line. The last battleship-versus-battleship action in history.

darter.name: Cdr David H. McClintock & Cdr Bladen D. Claggett
darter.role: Commanding officers, USS Darter and USS Dace
darter.bio: Working as a pair in the Palawan Passage, they made the first contact report on Kurita and sank two heavy cruisers and crippled a third before Darter grounded on Bombay Shoal. Dace took off her entire crew.
